title: Review: Free-radical substitution; Alkenes: electrophilic addition
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: OR07#t3 term and clue written for the game; OR12#t3 term and clue written for the game; OR07#t4 term and clue written for the game; OR12#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: OR07#N.9, OR12#N.14, OR07#N.12, OR12#N.16, OR07#N.6, OR12#N.11, OR07#N.2, OR12#N.2, OR07#N.14, OR12#N.6. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Propagation
items.clue: Chain stage in which the reactive species is regenerated, so the two steps repeat.

items.label: Carbocation
items.clue: A species containing C⁺ with only three bonds, formed after the C=C attacks Hδ+ or Brδ+.

items.label: Termination
items.clue: Stage in which two reactive species combine and are removed, e.g. giving a trace of ethane.

items.label: Bromine water
items.clue: Orange test reagent that turns colourless when shaken with an alkene but stays orange with an alkane.

questions.stem: 2,2-dimethylpropane, C₅H₁₂, reacts with chlorine in UV light. Four steps of the mechanism are: P: C₅H₁₁• + Cl₂ → C₅H₁₁Cl + Cl• Q: Cl₂ → 2Cl• R: C₅H₁₁• + Cl• → C₅H₁₁Cl S: C₅H₁₂ + Cl• → C₅H₁₁• + HCl Which sequence gives initiation, then the two propagation steps in the order they happen, then termination?

options.text: Q, P, S, R
S, Q, P, R
Q, S, P, R
Q, S, R, P

questions.explanation: Q makes Cl•. In S, Cl• removes an H atom, giving C₅H₁₁•. In P, that radical takes a Cl atom from Cl₂ and regenerates Cl•. R, two radicals combining, is termination.

questions.stem: Ethene reacts with hydrogen bromide by electrophilic addition. Which describes the curly arrows in the first step of the mechanism?

options.text: From the H atom of HBr to the C=C bond, and from Br to the H–Br bond
From the C=C bond to the Br of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to the H
From the C=C bond to the H of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to Br
Fish-hook arrows split H–Br into H• and Br•, which add to C=C

questions.explanation: The electron-rich C=C bond donates a pair to the δ+ H atom, forming a C–H bond, while the H–Br bonding pair moves onto Br. This gives CH₃CH₂⁺ and Br⁻; Br⁻ then bonds to the carbocation.

questions.stem: The products of the reaction of methane with chlorine in UV light include CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄. How are most of these more highly substituted products formed?

options.text: Cl• removes an H atom from a chloromethane; the radical then reacts with Cl₂
Cl• replaces an H atom in a chloromethane directly, releasing a free H• radical
Chlorinated methyl radicals combine with Cl• in termination, the main source of products
Each forms in one step, e.g. CH₃Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + HCl, as its equation shows

questions.explanation: Cl• attacks C–H bonds in chloromethanes as it does in methane: CH₃Cl + Cl• → CH₂Cl• + HCl, then CH₂Cl• + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + Cl•. Repeating gives CHCl₃ and CCl₄.

questions.stem: In the dark, at room temperature, but-2-ene quickly decolourises a solution of iodine monochloride, ICl. Butane does not react with it. The product is CH₃CHICHClCH₃. Which statement explains why but-2-ene reacts without light?

options.text: The C=C bond is weaker than a C–C single bond, so it breaks easily without needing any light.
The electron-rich C=C donates a pair to Iδ+, and the I–Cl bond breaks heterolytically.
ICl splits into I• and Cl• radicals even in the dark, and these radicals attack only C=C bonds.
The carbon atoms of the C=C bond are electron-deficient, so they attract the Clδ− end of ICl.

questions.stem: Methane reacts with bromine in ultraviolet (UV) light. Which equation represents the initiation step?

options.text: Br₂ → Br⁺ + Br⁻
CH₄ → CH₃• + H•
Br₂ → Br• + Br•
CH₄ → CH₃⁻ + H⁺

questions.explanation: UV light breaks the Br–Br bond homolytically: one electron of the bonding pair goes to each atom, giving two bromine radicals.

questions.stem: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂, reacts with hydrogen bromide. What is the product?

options.text: (CH₃)₂CBr–CBr(CH₃)₂
(CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)CH₂Br
(CH₃)₂CH–CH(CH₃)₂
(CH₃)₂CH–CBr(CH₃)₂

questions.explanation: HBr adds across C=C: H to one carbon, Br to the other. The double bond becomes single. Both carbons are alike, so there is one product, 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane.

questions.stem: Which statement about the chlorine radical, Cl•, is correct?

options.text: It has a 1− charge, which the dot is there to show.
It has eight outer electrons, all paired, like the chloride ion.
It is neutral, with seven outer electrons, one of them unpaired.
It is unreactive, as it has only one unpaired electron.

questions.explanation: Chlorine has seven outer electrons: three pairs and one unpaired electron. The dot marks the unpaired one. There is no charge.

questions.stem: Which set contains only species that can act as electrophiles?

options.text: H⁺, NO₂⁺, OH⁻
Br₂, HBr, NH₃
H⁺, NO₂⁺, Br₂
NO₂⁺, H⁺, Cl⁻

questions.explanation: Each can accept an electron pair. H⁺ has no electrons, NO₂⁺ is positive and electron-deficient, and Br₂ accepts a pair from a C=C bond.

questions.stem: A mixture of methane and chlorine does not react in the dark. A single brief flash of UV light splits a few Cl₂ molecules, yet many CH₃Cl molecules form for each Cl₂ split. Which explains this?

options.text: The flash heats the gas, and the hot gas keeps reacting after the light stops.
UV light breaks C–H bonds in methane, and each H• released starts a new reaction.
Each Cl• formed swaps places with one H atom in methane and is then used up.
Each Cl• starts a chain, as propagation regenerates Cl• again and again.

questions.explanation: CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl, then CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•. The chain repeats many times until two radicals meet in termination.

questions.stem: Ethene is bubbled through a solution of bromine in an organic solvent at room temperature, in the dark. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bromine loses its colour as CH₂BrCH₂Br forms by addition.
The bromine loses its colour as CH₂=CHBr forms by substitution.
No reaction occurs, as Br₂ has no positive charge.
No reaction occurs, as UV light is needed to split Br₂.

questions.explanation: Br₂ adds across the C=C bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. The orange-brown colour of bromine disappears; this is the test for C=C.
